summary: In low-power networks, memory-constrained routers may only hold a few routes. This RFC defines an IPv6 routing header carrying a source route, so packets can be delivered when RPL stores most routes at a root node.

eli5.summary: Some tiny helpers cannot remember a map. So the message carries its own list of stops, and they just follow it.

questions: source routes in low power networks
what is the rpl source routing header
subtitle: A compact IPv6 source routing header that lets RPL deliver packets through routers too small to store routes.

tldr.problem: Some memory-constrained routers in low-power networks can keep only a few default routes, yet RPL still needs to deliver datagrams to arbitrary destinations through them.
tldr.mechanism: A new IPv6 Routing header type, the Source Routing Header (Routing Type 3), lists every hop of the path and can elide the address prefix shared with the Destination Address. It is used only between RPL routers inside one routing domain, and with tunneling when it covers only part of a path.
tldr.outcome: Routers can forward by following the header instead of storing routes. Strict hop-by-hop use, domain-edge filtering and a mandatory loop check address the problems that got the Type 0 Routing header deprecated.

facts.label: Address entry size
facts.value: 16 - CmprI octets (16 - CmprE for the last)

today: RFC 6554 is a Proposed Standard from March 2012. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant for use alongside RFC 6550.

sections.title: Why a Source Route Header
sections.content:
The Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL, RFC 6550) is a distance vector IPv6 routing protocol for networks short on data rate, processing power, energy and memory. In some configurations, memory limits mean a router keeps only a small number of default routes and no other destinations, yet it must still forward datagrams.

In one RPL deployment model, more capable routers collect routing information and compute paths to arbitrary destinations. To deliver datagrams along those paths through the weak routers, RPL relies on source routing. This RFC specifies the Source Routing Header (SRH) for use strictly between RPL routers in the same RPL routing domain: a collection of RPL routers under a single administration. Network management sets the domain's boundaries by marking some links as exterior, or inter-domain, links.
sections.eli5: Small devices cannot memorize every road. A bigger device works out the route and writes it on the package so the small ones only need to read it.

sections.title: How the SRH Differs from RH0
sections.content:
The SRH is modeled on the Type 0 Routing header (RH0) of RFC 2460, which was deprecated for security reasons in RFC 5095. It adds a way to compact the addresses when all entries share a prefix with the packet's IPv6 Destination Address, which saves scarce channel capacity.

To avoid RH0's problems, three rules apply. First, a strict source route: every IPv6 hop between the source and destination of the route is listed. Second, the SRH is used only between RPL routers in a domain, and RPL Border Routers do not let datagrams already carrying an SRH enter or leave the domain. Third, a RPL router drops datagrams that include multiple addresses assigned to any of its own interfaces, to avoid forwarding loops.

The SRH is not protected by the RPL message security mechanisms of RFC 6550, and this document adds no confidentiality, integrity or authenticity protection for it.
sections.eli5: An older version of this idea let strangers send packages on silly, endless trips. This version stays inside one neighborhood, lists every stop, and throws away any package that would go in circles.

sections.title: Where the Header Goes
sections.content:
There are two cases. In Case 1 the SRH names the complete path from source to destination, both inside the domain, so the router places the SRH directly in the datagram. In Case 2 the SRH covers only a subset of the path, for example when the source or destination is outside the domain, or when a router such as the border router inserts a route while forwarding. Then the router uses IPv6-in-IPv6 tunneling (RFC 2473) and places the SRH in the outer IPv6 header.

Tunneling delivers the original datagram unmodified and makes ICMP errors return to the source of the SRH rather than the source of the original datagram. A router that is the source of a packet whose destination is in the same domain SHOULD include the SRH directly. Otherwise it MUST tunnel. The outer header and SRH are added and removed by the RPL router.

One use case has all RPL traffic flow through a Border Router. Between a source and the border router, packets follow the RPL DAG without an SRH. The border router then encapsulates them and adds an SRH in the outer header to reach the destination.

When tunneling, the router MUST set Segments Left to less than the original Hop Limit. If the route is longer than the Hop Limit, only the initial hops are included. It then decrements the original Hop Limit by the Segments Left value, so ICMPv6 Time Exceeded errors occur as on a traditional IPv6 network.
sections.eli5: If the list covers the whole trip, it goes on the package. If it covers only part, the package is put inside a bigger envelope with the list on the outside, so the original package is never touched.

sections.title: The SRH Format
sections.content:
The SRH has the same basic layout as RH0, with the Routing Type set to 3. Its fields are Next Header, Hdr Ext Len (in 8-octet units, not counting the first 8 octets), Routing Type, Segments Left, then CmprI, CmprE, Pad and a Reserved field, followed by the address vector Addresses[1..n].

Segments Left is the number of listed intermediate nodes still to be visited, and the originator sets it to n. The originator puts the first hop's address in the IPv6 Destination Address and the second hop as Address[1].

Compaction works like this. CmprI (4 bits) is the number of prefix octets elided from each of entries 1 through n-1, and CmprE (4 bits) is the number elided from the last entry. So entries 1 to n-1 are (16 - CmprI) octets long and entry n is (16 - CmprE) octets. Pad (4 bits) counts unused octets after Address[n], and it MUST be 0 when both CmprI and CmprE are 0. Reserved MUST be zero on send and ignored on receipt. With full addresses, the only difference from RH0 is the Routing Type value.

The SRH MUST NOT specify a path that visits a node more than once. The source MUST at least ensure that no address repeats and that the IPv6 Source and Destination addresses of the encapsulating datagram do not appear in the SRH. Multicast addresses MUST NOT appear in an SRH or in the Destination Address of a datagram carrying one.
sections.eli5: The header has a little counter of stops left. To save space, it can leave out the front part of each address when all the stops are on the same street.

sections.title: Processing at Each Router
sections.content:
As in RFC 2460, a routing header is examined only at the node named in the IPv6 Destination Address. If Segments Left is 0, processing continues with the next header. Otherwise the router computes n from the header length, Pad, CmprI and CmprE. If Segments Left is greater than n it sends an ICMP Parameter Problem, Code 0, and discards the packet. Otherwise it decrements Segments Left, finds the next address, discards the packet if that address or the Destination Address is multicast, swaps the next address with the IPv6 Destination Address, and checks the Hop Limit before forwarding with the Hop Limit decremented by 1.

Two further checks apply. If the new Destination Address is not on-link, the router MUST drop the datagram and SHOULD send ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable (Type 1) with Code 7, meaning the strict source route cannot be satisfied. To detect loops, a router MUST drop the packet and SHOULD send an ICMP Parameter Problem, Code 0, if the SRH contains multiple addresses assigned to its interfaces separated by at least one address not assigned to it. The RFC notes this adds significant per-packet overhead but is required to mitigate the bandwidth exhaustion attacks that led to RH0's deprecation.

RPL routers also keep the SRH inside the domain. Datagrams destined for a RPL router are processed normally, and a tunnel endpoint removes the outer header along with the SRH. Datagrams for elsewhere in the domain are forwarded. Datagrams destined outside the domain are dropped if the outermost IPv6 header contains an SRH not generated by the forwarding router.
sections.eli5: Each stop crosses off the next name on the list and passes the package on. If the next name is not a real neighbor, if the list goes in circles, or if the package has run out of travel time, the stop throws it out and sends back a note.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 5095 deprecated RH0 because of attacks such as bypassing filtering devices, reaching otherwise unreachable systems, network topology discovery, bandwidth exhaustion and defeating anycast. Since the SRH is only for use within a RPL routing domain, and RPL routers MUST drop datagrams entering or leaving the domain that contain an SRH, those attacks cannot be mounted from outside the domain.

They can still be mounted from inside. The RFC mitigates bandwidth exhaustion with the mandatory loop check. It judges filter bypass and reaching unreachable systems less relevant in mesh networks, whose topologies are highly dynamic, but admits that these and other attacks can occur within a domain. The SRH has no confidentiality, integrity or authenticity protection.

ICMPv6 error generation could be abused for denial of service by sending error-causing SRHs back to back. An implementation that correctly follows Section 2.4 of RFC 4443 is protected by ICMPv6 rate limiting.
sections.eli5: The list is only trusted inside the neighborhood, and anything with a list trying to cross the border is turned away. Inside, it is still possible for someone to misuse it, so rules against circles and a limit on error notes help.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
This document defines a new IPv6 Routing Type, the "RPL Source Route Header", assigned number 3 by IANA. It also defines a new ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable Code, "Error in Source Routing Header", assigned number 7.

The RFC also discusses MTU. To avoid fragmentation it is desirable to use MTUs of at least 1280 plus 40 for the outer IP header plus the maximum SRH size, but this needs Path MTU Discovery and the larger MTU may not exist on every link, such as 6LoWPAN links where it is 1280 octets. The RFC expects most traffic on these networks to be much smaller than the MTU, so the impact of fragmentation would be limited.
sections.eli5: Two numbers were reserved in a public list: 3 names this kind of header, and 7 names the error "the route list could not be followed".

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Type of the header that follows the Routing header.

fields.name: Hdr Ext Len
fields.desc: Length in 8-octet units, not including the first 8 octets.

fields.name: Segments Left
fields.desc: Listed intermediate nodes still to visit.

fields.name: CmprI
fields.desc: Prefix octets elided from entries 1 to n-1.

fields.name: CmprE
fields.desc: Prefix octets elided from entry n.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on send, ignored on receipt.
